data.text/markdown:
Guide to Pharmacology ligand cross-references: structure discrepancies

This notebook checks the ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem identifiers that the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY (GtoPdb) assigns to its ligands. For each cross-reference, it compares the standard InChI of the GtoPdb ligand with the one held by the linked database, and suggests an action for curators where they differ. It also explains why GtoPdb ligands do not match their ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem records in UniChem.

Summary

GtoPdb Version: 2026.3.1 - published: 2026-10-12; latest source retrieval 2026-11-17. Cross-references (sections 3 to 5). An exact record is a record in the linked database with exactly the GtoPdb structure: the one to link if the GtoPdb structure is right.
  • 20,468 ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem cross-references on 11,722 ligands were checked. 20,118 could be compared, and 19,506 of these match the GtoPdb structure exactly.
  • 182 identifiers have a problem of their own: malformed, retired or secondary, or a ChEMBL salt or child form where the parent may be intended (section 4). ChEMBL has an exact record for 9 of the 88 ChEMBL IDs that do not resolve to a compound.
  • 118 cross-references on 110 ligands differ in formula or connections (ChEBI 38, ChEMBL 35, PubChem 45; sections 5.1 and 5.2). An exact record exists for 67 of them.
  • 315 first differ in stereo (section 5.5): 40 have an opposite configuration, 13 define stereo differently on each side, and 262 define it on one side only. An exact record exists for 32 of the opposite configurations, and for 21 of the one-sided ones.
  • 140 first differ in hydrogens, 27 in charge or protons, and 3 in isotopes (sections 5.3, 5.4 and 5.6).
  • 13 cross-references on 11 ligands involve a metal-containing structure and require separate review. In 9 the InChIs differ. The other 4 lack a linked InChI (section 5.7).
  • On 30 ligands, all comparable records from at least two external databases share an InChI that differs from GtoPdb’s. These ligands merit review against the original evidence.
  • 11,158 of the 11,207 PubChem cross-references that agree with GtoPdb point to the compound that GtoPdb's own deposit is merged into, so the CID match alone does not independently confirm the GtoPdb structure (section 3). On 130 ligands, this is the only agreeing record while another database disagrees.
GtoPdb's own structures (section 6)
  • 300 ligands flagged as radioactive have an InChI with no isotope layer. Across all ligands, 221 InChIKeys occur more than once. 211 of those groups include a ligand flagged as radioactive. The isotope check also identifies 2 unflagged ligands with a radioisotope and 3 flagged ligands whose detected labels are all stable (section 6.1).
  • 19 ligands have a SMILES that is invalid (8) or does not reproduce their own InChI. The website draws structures from the SMILES (section 6.4).
  • 14 large peptides and oligonucleotides have an InChIKey but no InChI, so the InChI was rebuilt from the SMILES (section 6.3).
  • 36 inorganic ligands have no SMILES, InChI or InChIKey. For 30 of them, such as Na+, Ca2+, Cl- and NO, the name is the formula, so section 6.5 gives the structure. 6 of these have a suggested PubChem link added or replaced.
UniChem (section 7)
  • UniChem's own records (from its API) hold 6,050 GtoPdb ligands that have stereochemistry, and none of them keeps any of it: 6,049 are GtoPdb's structure with every stereo layer removed. Of 9,891 cross-references with identical stereo-defined InChIs, 6 appear in the UniChem mapping files. UniChem holds 187 groups of GtoPdb ligands differing only in stereo specification under shared UCIs (sections 7 and 7.2).
  • Where GtoPdb's SMILES and InChI differ in more than stereo, UniChem holds the SMILES structure for 2 of 2 ligands (section 7.1). Whether the stereo is missing from the file GtoPdb supplies or lost when UniChem loads it cannot be seen from public data; GtoPdb can check the file it sends.

How to reproduce

Everything comes from public sources. GtoPdb data come from its download files. UniChem data come from its flat-file mappings and from its API, which gives the structure UniChem holds for each GtoPdb ligand (section 7). ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem data come from their public APIs. Downloads and API responses are cached next to the notebook under data/raw_data/gtp_xref_audit/, so later runs only fetch identifiers that are not cached yet. Where that cache is missing, for example when the notebook runs on molab without the rest of its repository, it first copies the cache committed to the GitHub repository (about 17 MB), so it reproduces the published results without querying the APIs. Tick Re-download all source data only if you need to start from scratch: that downloads about 10 MB from GtoPdb and 130 KB of UniChem mapping files, then makes a few hundred ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem requests (a few minutes) and one UniChem request per GtoPdb ligand (about 14,000; around 10 minutes). Result tables are written to data/processed_data/gtp_xref_audit/ (section 8).
1. Data retrieval

data.text/markdown: Rows are the records in each download, or the IDs sent to each API. The UniChem mapping files have one row per pair of IDs that share a UniChem compound, so a GtoPdb ligand appears once for every ChEBI ID or PubChem CID it shares a structure with. For these files, IDs found counts distinct GtoPdb ligands. A ligand has several partners when ChEBI keeps as separate entries tautomers that standard InChI merges (it merges some tautomers, not all: Dhaked et al.), or when PubChem holds the same compound under several CIDs (vendor products, grades, E/Z names). A few PubChem groups mix stereoisomers, because UniChem holds both the GtoPdb ligand and some of its CIDs with their stereo removed (section 7). ChEMBL registers each structure once, so its mapping has one row per ligand.

2. How structures were compared

A standard InChI writes a structure as a series of layers, always in the same order, each adding detail to the ones before: formula (/C9H8O4), connections (/c), hydrogens (/h), charge (/q), protons (/p), stereo (/b, /t, /m, /s) and isotopes (/i). Each cross-reference is compared by reading the two InChIs from the left and stopping at the first layer that differs, since the later layers describe a structure the two records no longer share. Section 5 is organised by that layer. Standard InChI removes the bonds to metals, so a cross-reference where either structure contains a metal is a category of its own whenever the InChIs are not identical (section 5.7). The GtoPdb InChI is the InChI column of ligands.csv, or the InChI rebuilt from the SMILES where that column is empty (section 6.3). The linked record's InChI is the standard InChI that its own database provides. Three terms recur below:
  • Linked record: the ChEMBL, ChEBI or PubChem entry that a GtoPdb cross-reference points to.
  • Exact record: a record in the linked database whose standard InChI is exactly GtoPdb's, found by searching the GtoPdb InChIKey (xref_id_with_gtp_structure). It is the record to link if the GtoPdb structure is right.
  • Same parent after standardisation: the two records have the same largest organic fragment once it is neutralised and its isotope labels removed, either directly or as RDKit canonical tautomers. Apart from stereo means that the two parents differ only in stereo.
Each cross-reference gets a suggested action (suggested_action). It has one step for each identifier issue (section 4), then one for the structure, from the first of these rules that applies:
  1. GtoPdb already links an exact record as well: remove link.
  2. An exact record exists: replace link or change GtoPdb structure. Either the exact record is the right link, or the current link is right and the GtoPdb structure should change.
  3. The linked record has the structure of another GtoPdb ligand (other_gtp_ligands_with_xref_structure): remove link, since the identifier probably belongs to that ligand.
  4. Two or more external databases agree with each other but not with GtoPdb: check GtoPdb structure.
  5. Otherwise, the first layer that differs sets the step, or a metal in either structure does:
Section First layer that differs Step
5.1, 5.2 Formula or connections check which structure is intended
5.3.1 Hydrogens, same parent after standardisation keep link
5.3.2 Hydrogens, different parents check which structure is intended
5.4 Charge check which structure is intended
5.4 Protons keep link
5.5.1 Stereo, opposite configuration check GtoPdb structure
5.5.2 Stereo defined differently on each side review
5.5.3 Stereo, GtoPdb defines more keep link
5.5.3 Stereo, the linked record defines more check GtoPdb structure
5.6 Isotopes, only GtoPdb labelled keep link
5.6 Isotopes, only the linked record labelled check GtoPdb structure for a radioactive ligand, otherwise check which structure is intended
5.7 Any layer, with a metal in either structure check which structure is intended
5.7 None: the linked record of a metal-containing ligand has no structure review
A kept link always says why: how it differs, and whether the lookup found an exact record. Notes add context without changing the action. They say when:
  • an exact record is suggested, but the current link has another GtoPdb ligand's structure, or the external databases agree with each other but not with GtoPdb;
  • the only record that agrees with GtoPdb is the PubChem compound of GtoPdb's own deposit (section 3);
  • a radioactive ligand drawn without its isotope could not be searched for an exact record (section 5.6);
  • the linked record of a labelled ligand is unlabelled.
Section 8 describes the columns of the output tables.

3. How every cross-reference compares

The first InChI layer that differs from the GtoPdb structure, for every cross-reference, by linked database. Metal-containing counts comparable cross-references in section 5.7 whose InChIs differ. Not compared means that the GtoPdb ligand or the linked record has no structure (section 6.5 gives one for most inorganic ligands), or that the identifier could not be resolved (section 4). Agreement with PubChem is weaker evidence than it looks. GtoPdb deposits its own ligands in PubChem, and PubChem groups substance records (SIDs) whose structures standardise successfully under the corresponding compound (CID). For 11,158 of the 11,207 PubChem cross-references that agree with GtoPdb, the CID is the one that GtoPdb's own deposit (PubChem SID in GtoPdb's download) is merged into. A matching CID alone cannot establish independent corroboration. Other depositors may also contribute to the CID. Where such a CID is the only record that agrees with GtoPdb and another database disagrees, the suggested action says so.

3.1 Cross-references missing a standard InChI

These 184 cross-references on 175 ligands are the remaining links for which a structure comparison was impossible. The standard InChI is missing from GtoPdb alone for 39 links, from the linked record alone for 59, and from both records for 86.

data.text/markdown:
4. Identifier issues

This section lists identifiers that:
  • cannot be used as written (hidden characters, non-standard case, wrong database), or share a field with another ID;
  • no longer exist, or are secondary ChEBI IDs;
  • point to a ChEMBL salt or child form whose structure differs from GtoPdb's, where the parent compound may be the intended link.
A ChEMBL child form with exactly the GtoPdb structure, such as a salt or isotopologue that GtoPdb lists as its own ligand, is the right link and is not listed. difference shows how the linked structure compares with GtoPdb's; a cross-reference whose structure also differs is listed in section 5 as well. A ChEMBL ID that the molecule API does not return is checked in ChEMBL's ID lookup. This tells a retired compound (with the last ChEMBL release that contained it) from another kind of ChEMBL record, such as a document, and from an ID that was never issued. ChEBI's public data cannot tell a deleted ID from one that was never issued. For ChEMBL IDs that do not resolve to a compound, the suggested action names the exact record where there is one. In the tables of sections 4 and 5, structures draws the GtoPdb structure above the linked record's, each captioned with its ID, linked to the record, and its name. inchis gives both InChIs, GtoPdb's first, with the layer that differs first highlighted. The IDs in suggested_action are links too. The columns with the names and IDs, the other records the suggested action names, and each InChI on its own are hidden: the table's search still finds them, and its column panel shows them again.

5. Structure differences, layer by layer

Every cross-reference whose structure differs from GtoPdb's, by the first InChI layer that differs (section 2), except those with a metal in either structure, which are listed together in 5.7. A cross-reference that also has an identifier issue is listed in section 4 too. Where there is an exact record, the suggested action names it. chebi_stars is ChEBI's curation level: 3 means annotated by the ChEBI curation team, 2 means provided by a third party and not checked by ChEBI. 183 of GtoPdb's 1,602 ChEBI links (11%) point to 2-star entries, but 30 of the 38 that differ in formula or connections (79%) do.

5.1 Differs in formula

difference_detail gives both formulas, then what the records still share: the number of components where it differs (a salt or mixture), same atoms and connections where only the hydrogen count differs, and same parent after standardisation. A hydrogen count differs when a double bond is left out or a hydrogen is missing (drawn as a radical): VU0010010 (ligand 7633), for example, is drawn in GtoPdb without the C2=C3 double bond of its thieno[2,3-b]pyridine. tanimoto_similarity is the fingerprint similarity of the two structures. Where the linked record has the structure of another GtoPdb ligand, the suggested action names that ligand: the identifier probably belongs to it. Without an exact record, the suggested action removes the link.

5.2 Differs in connections

The records have the same formula, but their atoms are connected differently, for example a substituent at another position. difference_detail gives the part of each structure outside their largest common substructure, as SMILES with * where it bonds to the shared part. In structures, those atoms are highlighted in orange and the bonds joining them to the shared part in red. Structures above 60 heavy atoms, such as peptides, are too large for this search and are marked as not isolated automatically.

5.3 Differs in hydrogens

The records have the same atoms connected the same way, but place hydrogens, and with them double bonds, differently. The atoms whose hydrogen count differs are highlighted. difference_detail says whether the records have the same parent after standardisation (section 2).

5.3.1 Same parent after standardisation

Where the parents are the same only as RDKit canonical tautomers, the records are tautomers that standard InChI does not merge. Without an exact record, the link is kept.

5.3.2 Different parents

The parents differ even as RDKit canonical tautomers. The records may be tautomers that neither standard InChI nor RDKit recognises, such as an N-oxide drawn as an N-hydroxy imine, or different isomers, such as one with a double bond moved. The structures alone cannot tell which, so the curator checks which structure is intended.

5.4 Differs in charge or protons

The records carry different charges (/q) or have protons added or removed (/p): an acid against its conjugate base, or an ion against its neutral form. difference_detail gives the net charge of each record and how many more or fewer protons GtoPdb has. Without an exact record, a link that differs in protons is kept, and for one that differs in charge the curator checks which structure is intended. Before linking an exact record instead, check that the GtoPdb structure is the intended form. ChEBI keeps an acid and its conjugate base as separate entries on purpose, and GtoPdb's acetoacetic acid (ligand 4522), for example, is drawn as the acetoacetate anion. GtoPdb mostly stores one form per compound: 196 of its 11,590 ligands with an InChIKey are drawn with protons added or removed (InChIKey protonation flag other than N), and only 5 compounds are stored in two protonation states. In 26 of the 27 cross-references below, GtoPdb draws an ion and the linked record is neutral (ChEMBL 21, PubChem 3, ChEBI 2). 24 of these GtoPdb ions are drawn with protons removed and no counterion, like an acid drawn as its anion.

5.5 Differs in stereo

The records disagree about stereochemistry in one of three ways (stereo_relation):
  • Opposite configuration (5.5.1): both define the same stereocentres and double bonds, and at least one is inverted.
  • Defined differently on each side (5.5.2): each defines a centre that the other leaves undefined, or one defines more and a centre both define is written inverted.
  • Defined on one side only (5.5.3): one record defines every centre that the other does, and more, all written the same way.
Configurations are compared only in the first case, because next to an undefined centre InChI can write the same configuration inverted. Stereo created by isotope labels, such as a CHT group made chiral by tritium, is compared here when both records carry the same labels.
InChI writes a configuration relative to its numbering of the neighbouring atoms. For symmetry-equivalent atoms, such as the bridgeheads of a tropane or the two ends of a ring cis/trans pair in a 1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane, that numbering depends on the other centres. Next to an undefined centre, the same configuration can therefore be written inverted. Ricasetron (ligand 2302) and its PubChem record look like opposite configurations at both bridgeheads, yet defining the record's endo/exo centre gives exactly the GtoPdb InChI. Where both records define the same centres, the descriptors are compared centre by centre after applying the InChI /m inversion flag.

5.5.1 Opposite configuration

The records define the same stereocentres and double bonds, and at least one has the opposite configuration: enantiomer, epimer or diastereomer, E/Z isomer, or enantiomer or diastereomer where both leave the same centres undefined (an enantiomer if those are inverted too). Either the cross-reference points at the wrong stereoisomer, or the GtoPdb stereochemistry is wrong. Agreement among the comparable external records flags the GtoPdb structure and its links for review. Establishing the intended stereoisomer requires primary evidence.

data.text/markdown:
5.5.2 Stereo defined differently on each side

Each record defines a stereocentre or double bond that the other leaves undefined, or one defines more and a centre both define is written inverted. Next to an undefined centre, InChI can write the same configuration inverted (5.5), so the configurations are not compared: the two may be the same stereoisomer or different ones. The suggested action is to review them. difference_detail gives how many centres each record defines and how many are written inverted. It counts the centres and double bonds that either InChI lists; InChI does not list the undefined ones of a molecule or salt component that defines none.

5.5.3 Stereo defined on one side only

In 262 cross-references, one record defines stereo that the other leaves undefined, and every centre both define is written the same way. GtoPdb defines more in 194 and the linked record in 68; the table below shows that the direction depends on the database. These differences explain why exact InChIKey matching between GtoPdb and the linked databases fails. The missing stereo is a stereocentre (R/S), a double bond (E/Z), or ring cis/trans: the relative configuration of ring atoms that are not stereocentres, such as C1 and C4 of a 1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane. difference_detail says which record defines more, and missing_stereo what the other lacks. The centres defined on one side only are highlighted.

data.text/html:
GtoPdb defines more, and no exact record was identified (173). This includes 1 links where the radioactive ligand was stored without its isotope and the lookup was skipped (section 5.6). For 162 of the 164 PubChem links, PubChem's own standardisation removes the missing stereo from the GtoPdb structure (ring cis/trans 141, E/Z 16, R/S centre 3, E/Z + ring cis/trans 2; pubchem_standardisation_removes), reproducing the linked InChI.
PubChem's standardisation service was run on each GtoPdb structure. PubChem defines stereocentres by OEChem symmetry classes, which ignore ring cis/trans configuration. It also leaves E/Z undefined where the nitrogen of a double bond carries a carbon substituent (azo compounds, N-substituted imines), and stereo undefined at a phosphorus bonded to more than one O or S that may be charged or double-bonded, as in phosphorothioates (Hähnke et al. 2018).

5.6 Differs in isotopes

Only one record carries isotope labels, or the two carry different ones; difference_detail says which. A radioactive ligand that GtoPdb stores without its isotope (section 6.1) has the InChIKey of the unlabelled compound, so the linked database could not be searched for an exact record. Without an exact record, a labelled ligand's link to the unlabelled compound is kept, even where that compound is also a GtoPdb ligand, and the suggested action says that it is unlabelled.

data.text/markdown:
5.7 Metal-containing structures

Standard InChI removes the bonds to metals, writing a complex as its ligands and separate metal ions, and where the bonds to the metal were drawn changes the charges and hydrogens it writes. Auranofin (ligand 6306), for example, is written with Au+ and a thiolate in GtoPdb, but with neutral gold and a thiol in PubChem, so the two first differ in charge. The layers therefore cannot tell a different compound from the same one drawn differently. Every cross-reference where either structure contains a metal and the linked record does not have exactly the GtoPdb InChI is listed here instead of under its layer: 13 cross-references on 11 ligands. The alkali and alkaline-earth metals of salts, such as Na+ and Ca2+, do not count. difference still gives the first layer that differs. For 4 of them, the linked record has no structure at all, so structural agreement is unknown. Without an exact record, the suggested action is to check which structure is intended. 6. Structure issues within GtoPdb

6.1 Radioactive ligands stored without isotopes

GtoPdb flags 618 ligands as radioactive (its Labelled flag also covers fluorescent probes, which carry no isotope). Many have an InChI without an /i isotope layer. Omitting a label can give a radioligand the same InChIKey as its unlabelled parent. This table lists every InChIKey used by more than one GtoPdb ligand.

6.3 Ligands with an InChIKey but no InChI

GtoPdb gives 14 ligands a SMILES and an InChIKey but leaves their InChI empty. They are large peptides and oligonucleotides with 762–1,100 atoms (counting hydrogens), among the largest structures in GtoPdb. For 14 of them, the standard InChI rebuilt from the SMILES has exactly GtoPdb's InChIKey, so the audit uses that InChI for them. Without it, their cross-references could not be compared.

6.4 SMILES that disagree with the InChI

The GtoPdb website draws each structure from its SMILES (with the CDK); the InChI and InChIKey are separate fields. Regenerating the standard InChI from every SMILES with RDKit reproduces GtoPdb's own InChI for 11,557 of 11,576 ligands. The others are listed below, once per PubChem CID. 8 SMILES are not valid structures (RDKit's message names the atom whose bonds exceed its valence). The rest describe a different structure from the InChI, mostly double-bond or ring stereo that the InChI defines and the SMILES lacks. pubchem_cid_follows shows whether GtoPdb's PubChem compound has the structure of the SMILES or of the InChI: for 8 of the 11 PubChem links of ligands whose SMILES gives an InChI, it is the SMILES, consistent with GtoPdb's PubChem deposit being made from the SMILES. This check cannot find a SMILES that is wrong in the same way as its InChI. Diadenosine diphosphate (ligand 1065) is an example: its SMILES, InChI and IUPAC name all describe the 5',3'-linked compound, while its synonyms and its ChEBI entry are the 5',5'-linked one (section 5.2).

6.5 Inorganic ligands without a structure

GtoPdb has 39 inorganic ligands. 36 of them have no SMILES, InChI or InChIKey, so none of their cross-references can be compared. 30 of these are monatomic ions, small molecules or simple salts whose GtoPdb name is their formula, so the structure follows from the name. Monatomic ions such as Ca2+ and Cl- are read from the name; the other formulas are written out as SMILES in inorganic_smiles (appendix). The standard InChI and InChIKey were generated from these SMILES with RDKit. For 24 of these ligands, every ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem record that GtoPdb links already has exactly this InChI. The others have no cross-reference (5) or link a record with a different structure (1; see linked_records). pubchem_cid_with_structure lists the PubChem compounds with exactly the InChI shown, found by InChIKey. The other 6 (Audien, Auphen, carboplatin, cisplatin, ruthenium red, SNP) are metal complexes. Standard InChI disconnects bonds to metals, so it cannot distinguish, for example, cisplatin from transplatin. They are not given a structure here.

data.text/markdown:
7. Why GtoPdb ligands do not match in UniChem

UniChem identifies a compound (UCI) by its full standard InChI and InChIKey. If UniChem held GtoPdb's structures as GtoPdb publishes them, a GtoPdb ligand and its correct ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem records would share a UCI. UniChem's API gives, for any compound ID of a source, the UCI and the standard InChI that UniChem holds for it. Every GtoPdb ligand was looked up (section 1), and the InChI UniChem holds was compared with the InChI in GtoPdb's ligands.csv:

data.text/markdown: UniChem holds 11,589 of the 11,590 GtoPdb ligands that have an InChI; it does not hold flesinoxan (ligand 1). Among the 5,539 held ligands without stereo, 5,538 have identical InChIs. Of the 6,050 with stereochemistry, none keeps any stereo layer in UniChem: tetrahedral centres and E/Z double bonds are both gone, while isotope labels are kept (second table). The 2 other differences are explained in section 7.1. UniChem does use full InChIKeys. The second block of a standard InChIKey hashes the stereo and isotope layers. For 98.5% of the GtoPdb ligands with stereochemistry, UniChem's key has UHFFFAOYSA there, the hash of "no stereo or isotope layers", because UniChem holds no stereo for them and they carry no isotope label.

data.text/markdown: Valsartan shows what this does to UniChem's links. ChEMBL's CHEMBL1069 is held in UniChem with its stereocentre (/t22-/m0/s1), but GtoPdb ligand 3937, the same compound, is held without it. The two therefore get different InChIKeys and different UCIs, and UniChem cannot link them.

7.1 What UniChem's GtoPdb structures are built from

UniChem publishes the structures it holds, not the files its sources supply (it asks them for an SDF file or a SMILES table: UniChem provider examples). GtoPdb publishes each structure twice, as a SMILES and as an InChI, and for a few ligands the two disagree (section 6.4). These ligands show which of the two structures UniChem holds. The comparison leaves out stereo, since UniChem holds none for GtoPdb.

data.text/markdown: For 2 of these ligands, the SMILES and InChI differ in more than stereo: (3,5)-[19F]2-Phe-ψ-Ala (ligand 11370), Yoda2 (ligand 14004). Only one of the two can then match UniChem's structure, and it is the SMILES for 2 of 2. The other ligands cannot tell the two apart: their SMILES and InChI differ only in stereo, or the SMILES is invalid and UniChem holds the InChI's structure. This comparison identifies which published representation matches in the informative cases. The ChEMBL record for valsartan retains its stereo (CHEMBL1069 above). Whether the stereo is already missing from the file GtoPdb supplies or is lost when UniChem loads it cannot be seen from the public data. Suggested fix: GtoPdb should check that the file it supplies to UniChem carries the stereo: wedge bonds with 2D coordinates, or atom parities, in an SDF file, or isomeric SMILES in a SMILES table. GtoPdb should then ask UniChem to reload source 4.

7.2 Effect on UniChem's links

For cross-references whose structure is identical to GtoPdb's (section 3, identical), this table shows whether UniChem's mapping files pair the GtoPdb ligand with the same identifier. Where GtoPdb has stereochemistry, UniChem typically links GtoPdb to the unspecified-stereo entry (for valsartan, PubChem CID 5650 rather than 60846) or to nothing.

data.text/markdown: GtoPdb ligands that UniChem holds as one compound. UniChem files 382 UCIs under more than one GtoPdb ligand (826 ligands). In 195 of them GtoPdb's own InChIs are identical too; 186 of these include a ligand flagged as radioactive, the duplicates of section 6.1. In the other 187, GtoPdb's InChIs differ only in stereo, so UniChem merges stereoisomers that GtoPdb keeps apart. In 84 of them one ligand leaves the stereo undefined and another defines it, such as (±)-YM796 (ligand 285) and (−)-YM796 (ligand 287); in the other 103, every ligand carries stereo information and the group contains at least two distinct InChIs. They are listed below, one row per ligand.

8. Output files

Every run writes the tables below. curation_issues.csv is the file for curators: one row per cross-reference whose identifier has a problem or whose structure differs from GtoPdb's, with links to both records. Rows follow the order of sections 4 and 5: identifier issues on structures that could not be compared or that agree with GtoPdb first, then the layers in InChI order, then the metal-containing structures. Its main columns:
Column Meaning
first_difference The first InChI layer that differs (section 2)
difference The layers both records share up to that point and the one that differs, such as Shares formula, connections and hydrogens; differs in stereo. Layers neither record has, such as the charge of two neutral compounds, are not named
difference_detail How that layer differs; each part of section 5 says what it gives
stereo_relation, more_stereo_in, missing_stereo How the stereo differs, which record defines more, and what the other lacks (section 5.5)
metal_differs Whether either structure contains a metal and the InChIs are not identical (section 5.7)
xref_id_with_gtp_structure The exact record: a record in the linked database with exactly the GtoPdb structure
action The kind of each step of the suggested action, such as keep link or check GtoPdb structure
suggested_xref_id The ID to link instead, if any
suggested_action The steps and notes, as sentences
tanimoto_similarity Morgan (radius 2) fingerprint similarity of the two structures
other_gtp_ligands_with_xref_structure Other GtoPdb ligands whose structure matches the linked record
external_consensus_differs Whether two or more external databases agree with each other but not with GtoPdb

data.text/markdown:
Appendix: the functions used above

The notebook defines every function it uses here, so it runs on its own (in molab, or as a single file). They are marimo top-level functions, so from gtp_chemistry_problem import classify_inchi_pair imports them, as the tests in tests/ do. Shared constants, such as the InChI layers and the identifier patterns, are in the setup cell at the top.

Retrieval

Downloads and API calls (GtoPdb, UniChem, ChEMBL, ChEBI, PubChem), cached under data/raw_data/. Where that cache is missing, seed_cache first copies the one committed to the GitHub repository.

Identifiers

ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem identifiers: normalising them and finding what is wrong with them. Also GtoPdb's HTML names.

InChI layers

InChI layers and stereo, read from standard InChI strings (no RDKit).

RDKit helpers

RDKit structure helpers.

Structure drawings

Structure drawings: single molecules, and pairs laid out alike with their differences highlighted.

Tables

marimo tables with GtoPdb, ChEMBL, ChEBI and PubChem IDs shown as links.

Structure comparison and suggested actions

How a linked record's structure compares with the GtoPdb ligand's, layer by layer, and the suggested action.

UniChem checks

UniChem checks: how UniChem holds GtoPdb's structures.
